name: Python
fit: Automating work, working with data, and building prototypes or APIs.
why: A readable syntax and a broad ecosystem let you get useful scripts working quickly.
tradeoff: CPU-heavy loops may need optimized libraries or another language; distributing desktop apps takes extra packaging work.
example: Rename and organize files, analyze a CSV, or build a small bot.

name: JavaScript
fit: Interactive websites, browser tools, and event-driven services.
why: Runs in browsers; server runtimes let you reuse language skills for APIs and bots.
tradeoff: Dynamic types can hide mistakes until runtime. Browser and server APIs differ.
example: Build an interactive character sheet or a Discord bot using a suitable library.

name: TypeScript
fit: Growing JavaScript projects with shared data models and multiple contributors.
why: Adds static checks and editor help to JavaScript, making refactoring easier.
tradeoff: Needs a build or execution setup; types do not validate incoming data at runtime.
example: Build a web dashboard with shared types between its UI and API.

name: SQL
fit: Querying, joining, summarizing, and updating relational data.
why: Expresses database operations directly; pair it with your application language.
tradeoff: Database dialects differ. Indexes and query plans matter as data grows; use parameterized queries for application input.
example: Find overdue inventory items or summarize session attendance.

name: C#
fit: Desktop apps, .NET web services, and games using compatible engines.
why: Static types, mature tooling, and the .NET ecosystem suit substantial applications.
tradeoff: UI framework and deployment choices affect platform support. Engine APIs are a separate thing to learn.
example: Build a Windows utility or a game prototype with a C#-compatible engine.

name: Go
fit: Network services, command-line tools, and concurrent infrastructure utilities.
why: A compact language and built-in concurrency tools suit services with many independent operations.
tradeoff: Garbage collection and ecosystem fit still matter; it is not usually the first choice for rich desktop UIs.
example: Create a small service that monitors endpoints and reports failures.

name: Rust
fit: Performance-sensitive tools and systems where memory safety matters.
why: Ownership and strong compiler checks help prevent many memory and concurrency errors in safe code.
tradeoff: The ownership model adds learning time. Unsafe code and external libraries still need careful review.
example: Build a fast file-processing CLI or a small systems component.

name: PHP
fit: WordPress plugins, server-rendered websites, and PHP-based web applications.
why: Fits existing PHP hosting and WordPress directly; large framework ecosystems support web development.
tradeoff: WordPress hooks and APIs take learning. Browser interaction still requires JavaScript.
example: Add a custom WordPress dashboard or a form-processing endpoint.

name: Bash
fit: Short Linux or Unix scripts that connect existing command-line tools.
why: Useful for repeatable maintenance and pipelines without building a full application.
tradeoff: Quoting and error handling need care. For complex data or large programs, consider Python or another structured language.
example: Back up a directory, run checks, or automate a repeatable build step.

name: Visual Basic .NET (VB.NET)
fit: Windows business utilities, forms-based desktop software, and maintaining existing Visual Basic .NET applications.
why: An approachable syntax with static types and access to the .NET runtime and libraries. Windows Forms can suit internal tools.
tradeoff: Microsoft focuses VB on established scenarios rather than new workloads. Check template and library support before starting; C# has broader coverage for new .NET projects. VB.NET is distinct from classic VB6 and Office VBA.
example: Build a Windows Forms inventory editor or extend an existing VB.NET business application.

name: C++
fit: Game engines, native desktop applications, embedded software, and performance-sensitive components.
why: Direct control over resources, native compilation, and an extensive ecosystem for engines and existing systems. Modern C++ supports abstractions such as containers and resource-owning types.
tradeoff: Memory safety, undefined behavior, build systems, and dependencies require care. Modern ownership patterns help, but the language does not automatically prevent every memory error.
example: Build a small native utility, extend a game engine, or work on an embedded component.
